---
title: "Regular workflow"
---

Your training now has its own repository and website, and a copy on your
computer that you can edit. This chapter shows you how to make edits in your repository. These are the steps you repeat **every time** you work on your training website: open your training repository in VS Code, preview it, make your changes, and publish them.

The figure below shows the steps you will follow:

![](images/workflow-overview-image.png){fig-alt="Workflow showing the regular editing and publishing steps."}

The [cheat sheet](#cheat-sheet) at the end of this chapter lists them
all in one table.

## Open your training

Each time you start working, open your repository in VS Code and make
sure you have the latest version.

1. Open VS Code. It usually reopens the repository you worked on last.
![](images/workflow-01-openrecent.png){width=80% fig-alt="Screenshot: Opening the repository from recent."}  
   If not, choose **File → Open Recent**, or **File → Open Folder...**
   and select your repository folder.   
![](images/workflow-02-openrepository.png){width=80% fig-alt="Screenshot: Opening the repository from file."}

2. **Get the latest version.** If you work together with others, they
   may have uploaded changes since you last worked. In the bottom-left
   corner of VS Code, click the circular arrows next to the branch name
   (**Synchronize Changes**). This downloads their changes to your
   computer.   
   ![](images/workflow-03-synchronizechanges.png){width=40% fig-alt="Screenshot: VS Code status bar with the branch name and the Synchronize Changes arrows."}

### Which part of your website are you working on? {#switch-branch .unnumbered}

Apart from having the latest version, you also need to make sure you're
working on the right part of your website. Your website has two kinds of
parts, and your repository keeps each one in its own **branch**:

- **main**: the landing page of your training.
- **release-** followed by four digits: one training instance. Your copy of the template comes with one example training instance: **release-0000**.

The bottom-left corner of VS Code shows the branch you're working on:

   ![](images/workflow-04-branches.png){width=60% fig-alt="Screenshot: VS Code status bar showing the branch name main."}
 
Branches are explained in more detail in
[Repository structure](repository-structure.qmd#branches).

Before you start editing, **always** check that you're on the branch you
want to change. To move to another branch, see
[Switch branch](training-instances.qmd#switch-branch). 

For your first change below, stay on **main**.

## Preview your website

You're now ready to start editing. Before you change anything, start a
**preview**: it shows your website in your web browser while you work,
and updates every time you save a file. That way, you see straight away
what each change does.

The preview runs on your own computer, so only you can see it. Nothing
is published until you decide to, so you can check every change before
your collaborators or participants see it.

To start the preview, open a terminal (**Terminal → New Terminal**, see [Open a terminal](setup.qmd#open-a-terminal)) and run:

```bash
python scripts/preview.py
```

![](images/workflow-05-quartopreview.png){fig-alt="Terminal displaying command 'quarto preview'"}

Quarto now builds your website. After a few seconds, it automatically opens in your
web browser. 

![](images/workflow-06-previewinbrowser.png){width=75% fig-alt="Landing page displayed locally in a web browser using Quarto preview."}

If it doesn't open by itself, copy the address shown in the
terminal, for example `http://localhost:4123/`, and paste it into your
browser.

Keep the preview running while you work. To see a change, save the file
you edited: press **Cmd+S** (macOS) or **Ctrl+S** (Windows and Linux).
The preview in your browser then updates by itself.

To **stop the preview** when you are done editing, click in the terminal and press **Ctrl+C**.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Want to run another command while the preview is running?

The terminal running the preview is busy, so you can't type other
commands in it. Open a second terminal with **Terminal → New Terminal**,
and run your command there.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Another way to start the preview: the Preview button

When a page file (ending in `.qmd`) is open in VS Code, you can also
click the **Preview** button in the top-right corner of the editor. 

![](images/workflow-07-previewbutton.png){width=85% fig-alt="Screenshot: VS Code showing the Preview button."}

The website then opens inside VS Code. To see it in your browser instead, click **Open in Browser**.

![](images/workflow-08-openinbrowser.png){width=75% fig-alt="Screenshot: VS Code showing the open in browser button."}

:::

## Make a change

With the preview running, you will now make your first change: adding the title of your training. You will then publish this change, so you go
through the whole process once from start to finish.

Almost everything on your website comes from the files in the `data`
folder: the training title, dates, team, schedule, and so on. You change your
website by changing these files, without touching any code. How these files are organised is explained in [Repository structure](repository-structure.qmd). 

To change the title of your training:

1. In the Explorer panel, open the `data` folder and click `course.yml`.

   ![](images/workflow-09-datafolder.png){width=30% fig-alt="Screenshot: VS Code showing the explorer panel with data folder"}

2. Scroll down a bit and find the line:

   ```yaml
   title: "Training title"
   ```

3. Change the text between the quotation marks to your training's title, for example:

   ```yaml
   title: "Introduction to R"
   ```

   ![](images/workflow-10-changetrainingname.png){width=80% fig-alt="Screenshot: VS Code showing course.yml and training title change."}

4. Save the file with **Cmd+S** (macOS) or **Ctrl+S** (Windows and
   Linux).

The new title now appears at the top of the website preview in your browser.

![](images/workflow-11-changedtrainingtitle.png){width=80% fig-alt="Screenshot: Updated title in the preview."}

## Commit and push your changes

Your new title now shows in the preview, but only on your computer: it
isn't on your public website yet. To publish it, you send your change to
GitHub. This takes two steps, both in the **Source Control** panel of VS
Code:

- **Commit**: save a version of your changes, with a short description of
  what you changed. Each commit is kept, so you can always see what
  changed and when.
- **Push**: upload your commits to GitHub. GitHub then updates your
  website automatically.

To commit and push your change:

1. Click the **Source Control** icon on the left side of VS Code. Your
   changed files are listed under **Changes**.

   ![](images/workflow-12-sourcecontrol.png){width=35% fig-alt="Screenshot: Source Control panel showing the changed files."}

   ::: {.callout-note}
   ## More files than you changed?

   You changed only `course.yml`, but you probably see more files, for
   example in the `_generated` folder. That's expected: while the
   preview runs, the template updates these files automatically from
   your data files. Depending on what you change, you may also see
   `README.md`, `CITATION.cff` or `.zenodo.json`.

   Always commit **all** changed files together.
   :::

2. Hover over the word **Changes** and click the **+** next to it
   (**Stage All Changes**). This tells VS Code to include all changed
   files in your commit. They move to **Staged Changes**.  
  ![](images/workflow-13-stagedchanges.png){width=35% fig-alt="Screenshot: Source Control panel showing staged changes."}

3. In the **Message** box at the top, describe your change, for example
   `Change the training title`.  
  ![](images/workflow-14-commitmessage.png){width=35% fig-alt="Screenshot: Source Control panel showing staged changes with commit message."}

4. Click **Commit**.

5. Click **Sync Changes** to push your commit to GitHub.   
  ![](images/workflow-15-syncchanges.png){width=35% fig-alt="Screenshot: Sync Changes button."}

::: {.callout-note}
The first time you push, VS Code may ask you to sign in to GitHub. Follow
the instructions in your browser, then return to VS Code.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Changed something by mistake?

**Before** you commit, you can undo all changes to a file: in the Source
Control panel, hover over the file and click the curved arrow
(**Discard Changes**). The file goes back to how it was at your last
commit.  
 ![](images/workflow-16-discardchanges.png){width=35% fig-alt="Screenshot: Discard Changes button."}

You only need to do this for the files you changed yourself, such as
`data/course.yml`. The files the template updates automatically, for
example in the `_generated` folder, go back by themselves: as soon as
you discard your own change, the preview rebuilds them, and they
disappear from the list after a few seconds.

This only works while the preview is running. If they are still listed,
start the preview (`python scripts/preview.py`) and wait a few seconds.
:::

## Check the published website

After you push your local changes to GitHub to be published, GitHub rebuilds your training website by itself. This usually takes one or two minutes. 

To follow it on GitHub:

1. Open your repository on GitHub and click the **Actions** tab.  
 ![](images/workflow-17-githubactionstab.png){width=75% fig-alt="Screenshot: Github actions tab."}

2. Wait until both of these show a green checkmark:
   - **deploy-landing** (or **deploy-instance**, when you changed a
     training instance): builds your website;
   - **pages build and deployment**: publishes it.  

   ![](images/workflow-18-pagesbuilddeployment.png){width=75% fig-alt="Screenshot: Actions tab with deploy-landing and pages build and deployment both green."}
   
   A yellow dot means it is still running.

3. Open your website with the link under **About** on your repository's
   main page, see [Add the website link to your repository](setup.qmd#about-link). 
   Still seeing the old version? Wait a minute and refresh the page.
   Browsers sometimes show an older copy for a short while.

## Cheat sheet

Every time you work on your training, follow these steps in this order.

| To... | Where | What to do | 
|---|---|---|
| 1. Open your training repository | VS Code | Open VS Code. If your repository isn't open, choose **File → Open Recent** | 
| 2. Get the latest version | VS Code, bottom-left corner | Click the circular 'sync changes' arrows next to the branch name | 
| 3. Check the branch | VS Code, bottom-left corner | Read the branch name: **main** for the landing page, **release-YYMM** for a training instance | 
| 4. Start the preview | Terminal (**Terminal → New Terminal**) | Type `python scripts/preview.py` and press **Enter** | 
| 5. Make your changes | Explorer panel | Open a file, usually in the `data` folder. Change only the text after the colon, and save with **Cmd+S** or **Ctrl+S** |
| 6. Stage your changes | Source Control panel (left side) | Hover over **Changes** and click **+** to stage all changed files, including files you didn't change yourself | 
| 7. Commit | Source Control panel | Type a short description in **Message** and click **Commit** | 
| 8. Push | Source Control panel | Click **Sync Changes** |
| 9. Check | GitHub, **Actions** tab | Wait for two green checkmarks | 
| 10. Stop the preview | Terminal running the preview | Press **Ctrl+C** |
